Chapter 4: Medication, Therapy, and the Ambivalence of Recovery.
Deciding to seek treatment for depression is rarely a simple choice, is it? For a lot of people, it’s a journey filled with hesitation, hope, and sometimes a bit of doubt. The idea that medication or therapy might help sounds promising, but, as you may have guessed, things are usually more complicated than that.
After years of trying to cope alone, finally starting antidepressants brought a strange mix of relief and confusion. Imagine discovering that a little pill could actually change the way you feel—on one hand, it’s comforting, but on the other, it can feel unsettling. There were good days, when the medication seemed to lift that heavy fog, making it possible to do the things that once felt impossible. Getting out of bed, going to class, chatting with friends—suddenly, these tasks didn’t seem so overwhelming.
But here’s something to pay attention to: the relief was never quite complete. Side effects lingered, and there was always this feeling of being "not quite herself." What if the medication was just masking her real self? Was the person she became while on antidepressants somehow less authentic? This tug-of-war made it tough to fully embrace the treatment, even though it offered some much-needed stability.
Therapy brought its own set of challenges. Opening up about her experiences, digging into the source of her pain—it was both exhausting and, at times, enlightening. Some therapists were truly compassionate and insightful, helping her make sense of her tangled feelings. Others, though, seemed distant or even a little judgmental, which just made her feel more alone.
The relationship with a therapist isn’t always easy. There’s this constant push and pull—wanting to be understood, but also afraid of being too exposed. Trust doesn’t come easily, and it can be lost in a heartbeat. Progress isn’t a straight line, either. There are moments of breakthrough, but also setbacks and days when giving up seems tempting.
And outside the walls of the therapist’s office, not much seemed different. The stigma around mental illness still shaped how people treated her. Friends and family tried to help, but many just didn’t know what to say, or pulled away out of uncertainty. Even as she made progress, that sense of isolation hung around.
The wider culture made things even more complicated. In America, the rise in antidepressant use brought both hope and controversy. For some, medication was a lifeline after years of silent suffering. But there were questions, too—about the nature of happiness, the growing role of medication in our lives, and what it means to be “authentic.”
But for anyone living with depression, these big debates often felt far away. The reality was just about getting through each day—doing whatever it took to survive. Choosing medication or therapy wasn’t about philosophy; it was about necessity.
Over time, recovery stopped being about finding a magical cure. Instead, it became about learning to live with depression. There were good days and bad, moments filled with hope and others shadowed by despair. The goal shifted—from erasing depression to managing it, from chasing perfection to accepting imperfection.
In this new reality, even the smallest wins—like a single tear-free day, a real conversation, or a moment of laughter—took on huge meaning. The journey didn’t have a clear finish line. But just having the willingness to keep going, to keep reaching out for help, became a real source of strength.
So, what’s the takeaway here? The experience of medication and therapy is rarely a simple triumph. It’s a complicated, sometimes contradictory path, full of mixed feelings and uncertainty. And yet, even in the messiness, the chance for relief—however imperfect—gives us a reason to keep hoping.
